title: Type
instruction: Set every word at a readable size with the three faces and the type scale.
intro: Three typefaces carry every word we publish: Inter Tight for headlines and big figures, Inter for reading and the interface, and Lora Italic for the words we quote. Each has a single job, so a reader can tell a headline from a quotation before reading either.

We set sizes in rem, a unit tied to the reader’s own text setting, which is 16 px unless they change it. A reader who enlarges text gets larger type everywhere, and no text on screen sets below 13 px.

rules.title: Keep each typeface to its one job.
rule: Inter Tight 800 sets titles, headings and big figures. Inter sets body text, the interface, labels, captions, tables and chart text, at 400, 600 and 700. Lora Italic sets only quoted words, such as a pull quote or a quote card, at 400, or at 500 on a quote card.

text: One face for each job lets a reader tell a headline from a quotation at a glance. The wordmark is drawn from Inter Tight 800, so our headings share its voice, and the page still reads as ours with the logo covered. Charts follow the same split: Inter Tight for titles, Inter for labels and numbers, and Lora Italic only for quoted words.
why.basis: Our locked identity rules; design judgment

correct.caption: The three faces at true size, each in its job: a heading in Inter Tight 800, a sentence, a button and a kicker in Inter, and our editorial commitment quoted in Lora Italic.

failure.caption: Fails the faces’ jobs. Set in Lora Italic, the heading reads as a quotation, and the reader looks for the person who said it.

specs.label: Quotation
specs.value: Lora Italic 400, and 500 on quote cards; fallback Georgia, serif

specs.label: Source
specs.value: Google Fonts, SIL Open Font License

builders: Load all three with one link: https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@400;600;700&family=Inter+Tight:wght@800&family=Lora:ital,wght@1,400;1,500&display=swap. Then set faces only through --oa-font-family-display, --oa-font-family-reading and --oa-font-family-quote.

rules.title: Take every size from the type scale.
rule: Set text in the fourteen styles of the scale, with no sizes between them. On a web page, display styles grow with the window from 390 to 1440 px wide, and every size is in rem so it follows the reader’s text setting. A fixed artboard, such as a card, an email or a social image, takes fixed sizes from the same scale: up to 600 px wide, each style’s phone floor, and from 1,200 px wide, its desktop ceiling. Print pieces set type in points.

text: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text asks that text grow to 200 percent with nothing lost. A size in rem grows with the reader’s text setting, which a size fixed in px ignores. Our fifth edition set every size in px, and when our audit doubled its root text size, no text on the page grew.

A card or an email has one width, so the window cannot pick its sizes. Taking them from the scale’s two ends keeps a 480 px card and a 1,200 px social image in the same family as the page around them.

correct.caption: The fourteen styles at true size. On a phone each sample shows its phone floor, the size an artboard up to 600 px wide takes, and on a wider screen its desktop ceiling, the size for artboards 1,200 px and wider. On a web page, display styles move between the two as the window grows.

failure.caption: Fails 1.4.4. Two columns as a reader sees them with text set to 200 percent. The column set in rem has grown to 34 px; the column set in px is still 17 px.

specs.label: Text size base
specs.value: 16 px, the browser default; every size is a multiple in rem

specs.label: On a web page
specs.value: Display sizes grow from 390 px to 1440 px wide

specs.label: Artboards up to 600 px wide
specs.value: Each style’s phone floor: title 56, section 44, figure 48, H3 26, H4 20, quote 24, intro 19, ask 19, body 17, body small 15, UI 15, caption 14, label 13, data label 13 px

specs.label: Artboards 1,200 px and wider
specs.value: Each style’s desktop ceiling: title 110, section 80, figure 104, H3 32, H4 24, quote 32, intro 22 px; the rest as on phones

specs.label: Artboards between 600 and 1,200 px
specs.value: Each style’s size from either column

specs.label: Print
specs.value: Points, with all text at 10 pt or larger; chapter 25 sets the point scale

builders: Set a style with its shorthand and its parts: font: var(--oa-type-body) carries face, weight, size and line height, and letter-spacing, text-transform and font-variant-numeric each have their own property, such as --oa-type-label-letter-spacing. On a fixed artboard, override only the size, as in font-size: 1.625rem for an H3 on a 480 px card. Never write a font size in px.

rules.title: Set no text on screen below 13 px.
rule: The smallest text on screen is 13 px, or 0.8125 rem: labels, tags and data labels. A label in capitals at 13 px takes Inter 700 with 6 percent tracking. A specimen that shows a mark or a minimum size at true size is a graphic, and its caption says so.

text: Our fifth edition set its labels at 10 to 12 px. Our census of its text, which measured 2,346 text elements rendered at 1440 px and left out text inside SVG drawings, counted 833 under 13 px. A floor with no screen exceptions keeps kickers, tags and navigation readable without zoom. At 13 px, capitals need less tracking than they did at 10 px, so 6 percent keeps them open without pulling a word apart.
why.basis: Design judgment; our measurements of the fifth edition, October 2026

correct.caption: Four labels at true size, all at 13 px. The location line is secondary text at 5.49 to 1; the column head, tag and data label are primary text at 13.29 to 1.

failure.caption: Fails the 13 px floor. A graphic at true size of two labels from our fifth edition: the chapter kicker at 11 px with 13 percent tracking, and the footer line at 10 px.

specs.label: Label
specs.value: Inter 700, capitals, 13 px, line height 1.4, +6% tracking

specs.label: Data label
specs.value: Inter 600, 13 px, line height 1.3, tabular figures

specs.label: Print floor
specs.value: Taglines 7 pt, capitals 3 mm in identity marks

builders: The shared check fails any text under 12.95 px, with SVG text measured at its rendered scale. A chart drawn in SVG has to keep its labels at 13 px on a phone, so draw a phone version rather than shrinking the desktop one.

rules.title: Tighten tracking only as headings grow.
rule: Tracking is the space added to or taken from every pair of letters. Display styles take negative tracking that eases as the size drops: −3 percent for titles, −2.5 percent for sections, −1 percent for H3 and −0.5 percent for H4. Big figures, which are digits, take −3 percent, and quotes in Lora Italic −2 percent. Reading styles keep the font’s own spacing, and labels in capitals open to +6 percent.

text: At display sizes the font’s own spacing leaves gaps a reader sees, and a little negative tracking closes them. Pulled too far, the letters touch. Our fifth edition used −4.5 percent at every heading size from 24 to 110 px, and at the cover’s 110 px that makes 7 of our tagline’s 24 letter pairs touch. At the title’s −3 percent, two do.
Across the 23 rule titles in chapters 05 to 07, set at the H3 size of 32 px, 107 of 738 letter pairs touch at −3 percent, the value an early draft of this guide used, and 32 at −1 percent.

correct.caption: An H3 at true size, 32 px with −1 percent tracking. Its word spaces measure 5.7 px, and one of its 28 letter pairs touches, where the arm of an r meets its neighbor.

failure.caption: Fails the tracking scale. The same heading at −3 percent, the H3 value in an early draft of this guide. Four of its 28 letter pairs touch, and its word spaces shrink to 5.0 px.

specs.label: Letter pairs that touch, tagline at 110 px
specs.value: 2 of 24 at −3 percent; 7 at −4.5 percent; 0 at the font’s own spacing

specs.label: Letter pairs that touch, rule titles at 32 px
specs.value: 32 of 738 at −1 percent; 107 at −3 percent; 4 at the font’s own spacing

builders: Tracking lives in each style’s letter-spacing property, in em, so it scales with the size: letter-spacing: var(--oa-type-h3-letter-spacing). Leave body text at the font’s own spacing.

rules.title: Line up figures in tables, and give negatives the true minus sign.
rule: Tables, trackers and chart labels set tabular figures, which give every digit the same width so a column lines up. A negative number takes the minus sign (−, U+2212), which matches the plus sign’s width, and the numbers in one column carry the same number of decimals.

text: A reader compares a column by its right edge, and proportional figures move that edge digit by digit. The hyphen is shorter than the minus and sits lower, so a hyphen before 245 can read as a dash. Chapter 02’s house rule H07 asks for the true minus in prose as well.
why.basis: Design judgment; chapter 02, house rule H07

correct.caption: A finding at true size, set in Inter with tabular figures. The figures align on the right, and the one fall, in information jobs, takes the true minus.

failure.caption: Fails the figure rule. The same table with proportional figures, columns aligned left and a hyphen for each minus. The digits no longer stack, and the two minus signs read like dashes.

specs.label: Minus sign
specs.value: − (U+2212); plus sign + (U+002B) where a sign is printed

builders: In a template, write the minus as − or \2212. A chart script should format negatives itself, since a number converted to text takes a hyphen.

rules.title: Balance a heading’s lines, and keep two words or more on its last line.
rule: A heading that runs to two or more lines splits into lines of near equal length, and its last line holds at least two words. Body text wraps so its last line holds more than one short word.

text: A lone word on a heading’s last line, called a widow, reads as an afterthought and pulls the eye down a line for one word. Balanced lines let a reader take in a heading at a glance.

correct.caption: A heading from our fifth edition’s type chapter at true size, its two lines balanced.

failure.caption: Fails the widow rule. The same heading wrapped by width alone, which leaves one word on its last line.

builders: Older browsers ignore text-wrap and wrap as usual, so check the longest real heading at 360 px and, where a widow appears, join its last two words with a no-break space.

rules.title: Hang opening quotation marks outside the text edge.
rule: In a pull quote or a quote card, the opening mark sits in the margin, so the first letter of every line starts on the same edge. Use curly quotation marks and apostrophes (“ ” ‘ ’), and keep common ligatures on and discretionary ligatures off.

text: When the mark sits inside the edge, the first line starts a mark’s width to the right of the rest, and the block looks indented by accident. Readers know curly marks from books and newspapers, so a straight mark looks like a typing slip.

correct.caption: Our editorial commitment as a pull quote at true size. The opening mark hangs 0.39 em into the margin, its measured width, and every line starts on the hairline.

failure.caption: Fails the hanging rule. With the mark inside the edge, the first line starts a mark’s width to the right of the second.

builders: Set hanging-punctuation: first where the browser supports it, and a negative text-indent of 0.39 em on the quote where it does not.

rules.title: Set body text at 60 to 75 characters a line.
rule: Set body text to a measure of 60 to 75 characters a line on wider screens, and intro text to 65 at most. A phone gives about 37 to 40 characters, which suits a small screen. Chapter 07 gives the column spans that deliver these measures at each width.

text: Lines far past 75 characters make the eye lose its place on the way back to the next one. The ch unit, the width of a zero, runs wider than Inter’s average letter, so an intro set to 65ch, as in our fifth edition, measured 78 to 83 characters a line when we set it at 22 px.
why.basis: Design judgment, with WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.8 (AAA, advisory)

correct.caption: The opening of our writing rules in chapter 02, at true size and the body measure, 33.88 rem. Its full lines measure 65 to 66 characters. Over 7,041 characters of chapter 02’s prose at the same width, lines average 64, and at the widest body measure, 71.

failure.caption: Fails the measure. The same paragraph as our fifth edition set its intros, at 22 px and 65ch. Its full lines run 78 to 83 characters, and the eye has far to travel back to the start of each.

specs.label: Body measure
specs.value: 33.88 rem, 542 px at 16 px text; lines average 64 characters

specs.label: Widest intro measure
specs.value: 41.91 rem; at 22 px, lines average 61 characters

specs.label: Phones
specs.value: About 37 to 40 characters at 360 and 390 px

builders: Cap a text block with max-width: var(--oa-layout-measure-body-ideal). The measure is in rem, so a reader who enlarges text keeps the same characters a line.

rules.title: Set email type in the system font stack.
rule: Many mail apps ignore web fonts, so email sets headlines and body text in Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, and quotations in Georgia Italic. An email is a fixed artboard 600 px wide, so it takes the scale’s phone floor sizes, as Rule 06.2 sets out. Chapter 22 shows the full template.

text: A mail app that cannot load a web font falls back to a face of its own choosing, often a serif. The system stack names the fallback in advance, so every reader sees a face we chose. Our fifth edition kept this rule and then set its own email headline in Inter Tight.

correct.caption: An email header at its true width of 600 px on White, set in the system stack: the headline in Helvetica or Arial at 26 px, the H3 floor, and the quote in Georgia Italic at 24 px, the quote floor.

failure.caption: Fails the email rule. The headline set in Inter Tight, which a mail app that cannot load the web font shows in its own default serif.

specs.label: Sizes
specs.value: The phone floor: headline 26 px, quote 24 px, body 17 px

builders: Write the stack on every text element of an email, inline, since many mail apps strip a style block. The wordmark goes in as an image with its name as alt text.

rules.title: Load the three faces, and let no other face stand in.
rule: Pages load Inter Tight, Inter and Lora from their published files, in the weights the scale uses. Arial and Georgia appear only as fallbacks inside the font stacks. No other face stands in for ours, including Spectral, Source Sans, Public Sans, IBM Plex, Libre Baskerville, Playfair Display, Cormorant, Helvetica Neue for display, Times New Roman, Calibri, Roboto, Open Sans and Montserrat.

text: Our locked identity rules say a font substitution is never a finished identity decision. A fallback’s one job is to keep a page readable when a font fails to load. Measured at 32 px, the heading here sets 498 px wide in Inter Tight and 504 px in Arial, 1.3 percent wider. A page that failed to load Inter Tight can look finished, and only the letters give it away. The list carries our fifth edition’s never-substitute list forward.
why.basis: Our locked identity rules; design judgment

correct.caption: A heading at true size in Inter Tight 800, 498 px wide at 32 px.

failure.caption: Fails the face rule. The same heading in Arial, the fallback that shows when Inter Tight fails to load. It sets 504 px wide, close to the original, and its letters lose the cut of the wordmark’s face.

builders: Use font-display: swap, as the Google Fonts link sets it, so text shows at once in the fallback and changes face when the file arrives. Ship the font license with any package that carries the files.

extras.label: Sizes for fixed artboards
extras.caption: Every style’s size on a web page and on a fixed artboard, such as a card, an email or a social image. Between 600 and 1,200 px, take each style’s size from either column. Print pieces set type in points, with all text at 10 pt or larger.
